Olympic Dreams - 2 Men in a Boat

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
South Africans sailors Alex Burger and Benji Daniel are on course for Tokyo, under the expert guidance of coach Asenathi Jim.

Unique Selling Point:
This is a uniquely South African story, uniting athletes from vastly different backgrounds through a common passion behind one goal - Olympic gold.
Beautiful visuals of boats in False Bay, skimming silently through the waves, driven by wind and the love of competition. Getting to know our team and their major competitors, to create the new interest in sailing and generate excitement about the Games for our viewers.

Summary:
Three hugely talented individual sailors have been brought together by the RaceAhead Foundation - started in 2008 by former Olympian Dave Hudson and his son Roger to get young, talented sailors competing in major world tournaments and proudly representing South Africa. They've had over 100 young sailors aged between 16 -23 in the program.

Further information:
Asenathi Jim:
When he was 8 years-old Asenathi's mom brought him from a small village close to Fort Beaufort in the Eastern Cape to spend his school holidays with her at work in Redhill, the small township above Simon's Town. To keep him busy, she sent him down to the Izivunguvungu sailing school iron by former Olympian Ian Ainslie. He was instantly hooked on the sport of sailing. He quickly progressed though the ranks and was invited to join the race Ahead Foundation, run by former Olympian Dave Hudson and his son Roger. RaceAhead is a NPO aimed at giving young sailors from all backgrounds the opportunity to compete in international regattas at a high level. Kim's talent was obvious. In 2010 he finished 9th out of 36 at the World Youth Championships in the 420 category. He then teamed up with Roger Hudson and successfully competed in the London 2012 Olympic Games and the Rio 2016 Olympic Games. Now aged 28 he has successfully moved to a more senior role of coaching and mentoring the RaceAhead squad. He has been assisting and coaching Alex and Benji since the start of their campaign in 2018, and brings an enormous amount of knowledge and experience to the young team.

Alex Burger
On a small dam close to Muizenberg, Alex started sailing lessons on Sunday afternoons with his family. It quickly progressed from a hobby to a passion to racing in the international youth divisions where he competed in junior world championships. He attracted the attention of RaceAhead and was invited to join in on the training sessions. n 2014 he was invited to team up with Asenathi and do a few events on the Olympic circuit to gain some experience. They placed well, and Alex was selected as first reserve fro Asenathi and Roger for the Rio 2106 Olympics. In 2018 Alex put his Engineering degree on hold to pursue an Olympic sailing campaign with Benji.

Benji Daniel
Benji was introduced to sailing by his parents to get him out of the house during the summer holidays.He spent his early teenaged years competing in local events and in 2017 Benji was invited to train with the RaceAhead squad. He quickly rose up the rankings and was paired with Alex Burger to compete in the 29er World Championships in Los Angeles. The 29er is the youth feeder class to senior 49er class. They trained together for a few days in Cape Town before flying to LA where they beat 129 other teams from 17 countries to win the World Champs. After completing his matrix in 2018, Benji decided to suspend the start of this mechanical Engineering degree at UCT to pursue an Olympic sailing career in the Men's 49er with Alex. In April 2021 the team successfully qualified South Africa for the Tokyo 2021 Olympics in Oman.

Script:


OLYMPIC SAILING


V/O: A crisp, clear day in Table Bay and racing though the water is the fastest 2-man skiff in the world. There are very few 49ers in South Africa and on board are two of our most skilful sailors.

But this vessel holds more than just a talented crew. It carries the Olympic hopes and dreams of an entire nation

Alex: We are going there with serious intentions of competing at the best of our abilities, because it’s the biggest sporting event in the world. And it is exciting and it is terrifying at the same time.

Benji: Just a combination of emotions that are very hard to explain. Like a lifelong goal reached.

V/O: Alex Burger and Benji Daniel have bagged one of only 19 spots on the starting line of the 49er class at the Tokyo Olympic Games. But where did their epic voyage begin?

Alex: When I was seven years old my parents came to me – and I was at quite a conservative Afrikaans primary school at the time – and they said to me: Alex, it’s Sunday today. Would you like to go to church or would you like to go to sailing lessons?

Derek: That’s quite a choice?

Alex: It was a very big choice. And I chose sailing because it was a really nice day outside, and I went to sailing lessons at the yacht club in Muizenburg.

V/O: For 20 year-old Benji it was a similar story in his hometown of Durban.

Benji: My parents put me on a holiday learn-to-sail course just to get me out of the house during school holidays. And it was the worst decision they ever made, I’ve been hooked ever since.

Alex: There are a lot of moving parts in a sailing boat, there’s so many ropes, and tensions and wires and weights and distributions and kind of research that needs to go around it. I mean the technicality, it’s fascinating you know. But at the same time you have to complement that with athleticism.
And then of course the human factor of having a teammate is also fascinating as well.

Benji: It’s just a fantastic thing to be out in the waves, in nature, just sort of fighting against nature to try and get around the course, which is quite a fantastic feeling. And then there’s the racing, which is very close and sort of nip & tuck, cut-throat which is also incredibly good fun.

Link: You might have childhood memories of messing around in boats, but this class called the 49er is not that sort of boat. It’s built for speed and performance and has been developed over the last 5 Olympic Games.

Alex: The mast where the sails go up has become longer, and the wings that stick up that we stand on when we sail later have become wider. So essentially the boat has become more powerful and faster and sleeker and fundamentally just you know a little bit more high performance.

00:02:47 There are two big factors: It’s how fast you can make the boat go, and can you make the boat go in the right direction and sort of sail the shortest distance at the highest speed possible? So you have to sort of develop both of those skills. And once you’ve become quite good at it you can then start winning races and regattas internationally.

V/O: And that’s exactly what happened when Alex and Benji first teamed up in 2017. They surprised themselves by beating over 120 competitors to win the Junior World Championships in the 29er class.

Alex: I think that was a great indicator of what we were able to achieve.
Without it, I don’t think we’d be here. But then again it is only a junior world championships. It means very little in the Olympic sailing season.

V/O: After matriculating in 2018 Benji decided to delay his University career to focus on sailing. Alex put his Mechanical Engineering degree at UCT on hold to devote himself fulltime to qualifying for Tokyo 2020. Their families have funded this campaign, and to give them the edge they’ve also hired double Olympian Asenathi Jim as their coach.

Link: Behind the Olympic dreams of Alex and Benji is a coach who has a wealth of experience. But his course hasn’t always been plain sailing.

V/O: Asenathi grew up in Fort Beaufort in the Eastern Cape with his grandparents. At the age of 8 he came to spend the school holidays, with his mother in Redhill township in the mountains above Simon’s Town. Even though he no longer lives here, it’s the place he calls home.

Asenathi: I feel so special and privileged to be coming from a place like this and to be where I am today. But I feel like this is a place where I belong.

V/O: To keep him busy, his mother sent him down the mountain to the naval base to join the Izivunguvungu Club where he learned to sail.

Asenathi: Fortunately enough, Ian Ainslie who’s a three-time Olympian started a sailing school, actually this club called Izivunguvungu Club….. which is an opportunity for disadvantaged kids.

Asenathi: We used to be launching from there and we basically had seven boats, and they were called bosuns. It’s an old navy boat. ….And I tried my best to sail every day because that’s something that I actually fell in love with.

Derek: But you were a scared?

Asenathi: No. I wanted actually to get on a boat. To me it was a ew challenge, and I love challenges as a person. To be on a boat is something very new, unusual, and I was like I’m going to take this opportunity. And from day one, I’m not going to lie, I’ve got taken by the sport.

V/O: Asenathi’s skill and passion for sailing was nurtured by the RaceAhead Foundation, which saw him successfully compete internationally as a junior. As a teenager he teamed up with Roger Hudson to compete in the London Olympics and later for Rio.

Derek: What has been the pinnacle, the most special moment in your sailing career?
Asenathi: In Barcelona, when we qualified for the London Olympics. We only started like 18 months before the London Olympics and for us to actually qualify for that event was actually a mind-blowing thing.

Derek: Tell us about Asenathi as a coach?

Alex: He drives the training regime and he makes sure that we don’t slack at any point…..He’s disciplined. He’s strong, he’s hard, but he’s good fun. And he is a good character and he’s a happy human.

Benji: He knows exactly what top level Olympic sailing requires, both on the water and off the water. So it’s great to have him as a mentor for on the water training and how to sail a boat better, how to race better, but also just sort of mind state and preparation and not burning yourself out.

Link: You may think that sailing is rather a laid-back sport, but at the top level when you’re going for the Olympics, you have to push yourself. And push some weights.

Benji: You have to be very strong in terms of your core to keep us like standing solidly on the boat, and to be able to pull ropes that have a reasonable unallowed without throwing yourself around. And when the boat moves you have got to stay solid. And often we are turning there’s quite a few G-forces trying to pull you out.

V/O: Alex and Benji will be up against the stiffest competition in the world. Reigning Olympic champions Peter Burling and Blair Tuke are veteran sailors from New Zealand, fresh from their resounding victory in the America’s Cup.

Derek: What are your hopes for them in Tokyo?

Asenathi: The moment counts more than the years that you put in. And the one thing I’ve learned about my team is that they can do things when it counts, and this counts for the nation, for us and for their families. We are going to give it everything we have.

V/O: While Alex and Benji streak across Table Bay in their practice boat, their racing boat is already on its way to Japan. The first event kicks off on the 27th of July at the Enoshima Yacht Club in Tokyo, and South Africa’s flag will be flying high.

Benji Daniel Benji was introduced to sailing by his parents to get him out of the house during the summer holidays.He spent his early teenaged years competing in local events and in 2017 Benji was invited to train with the RaceAhead squad. He quickly rose up the rankings and was paired with Alex Burger to compete in the 29er World Championships in Los Angeles. The 29er is the youth feeder class to senior 49er class. They trained together for a few days in Cape Town before flying to LA where they beat 129 other teams from 17 countries to win the World Champs. After completing his matrix in 2018, Benji decided to suspend the start of this mechanical Engineering degree at UCT to pursue an Olympic sailing career in the Men's 49er with Alex. In April 2021 the team successfully qualified South Africa for the Tokyo 2021 Olympics in Oman.
